Using scalar dipole–dipole coupling for the two induced dipoles,
\[
\mathbf p_i=\alpha_i\mathbf E_i(\mathbf r_i),
\]
the interaction energy in the far field \(kd_0\gg1\) is
\[
U_{\rm int}\simeq
-\frac{k^2\alpha_1\alpha_2E_1E_2}{4\pi\epsilon_0d_0}
\cos\!\left[k(z_1-z_2)+\Phi\right],
\qquad
\Phi=\phi_1-\phi_2+\frac{z_1^2-z_2^2}{2z_R}.
\]
Here the Gaussian-beam phase is
\[
\psi_i(z_i)=kz_i-\phi_i-\arctan(z_i/z_R),
\]
so the relative propagation phase along \(z\) is
\[
k(z_1-z_2)-(\phi_1-\phi_2)
-\arctan(z_1/z_R)+\arctan(z_2/z_R).
\]
For \(z_1,z_2\ll z_R\),
\[
\arctan(z_i/z_R)\simeq z_i/z_R,
\]
and the quadratic term in the interaction must be combined with the trap curvature term; this gives the longitudinal equilibrium condition. Expanding the interaction force about that equilibrium gives, to leading order in \(1/(kd_0)\),
\[
F_1^{(\mathrm{int})}
=-\frac{k^3\alpha_1\alpha_2E_1E_2}{4\pi\epsilon_0d_0}
\left(1+\frac{z_1+z_2}{2kz_R}\right)
\sin\!\left[k(z_1-z_2)+\Phi\right].
\]
Linearizing in the small relative displacement yields
\[
F_1^{(\mathrm{int})}\simeq
-(k_1+k_2)(z_1-z_2),\qquad
F_2^{(\mathrm{int})}\simeq
-(k_1-k_2)(z_2-z_1),
\]
with
\[
k_1=
\frac{k^4\alpha_1\alpha_2E_1E_2}{4\pi\epsilon_0d_0}
\sin\!\left(\phi_1-\phi_2\right),
\]
and
\[
k_2=
\frac{k^3\alpha_1\alpha_2E_1E_2}{8\pi\epsilon_0z_Rd_0}
\cos\!\left(\phi_1-\phi_2\right).
\]
Thus \(k_1\) is the reciprocal optical-binding spring, while \(k_2\) is the nonreciprocal contribution arising from the axial intensity/phase gradient of the Gaussian beams.

\[
\boxed{
k_1=
\frac{k^4\alpha_1\alpha_2E_1E_2}{4\pi\epsilon_0d_0}
\sin(\phi_1-\phi_2),
\qquad
k_2=
\frac{k^3\alpha_1\alpha_2E_1E_2}{8\pi\epsilon_0z_Rd_0}
\cos(\phi_1-\phi_2)
}
\]

Assume the two standing-wave pairs form the usual phase-controlled square lattice, with no residual cross-interference between the \(x\) and \(y\) pairs. Define

\[
k=\frac{2\pi}{\lambda},\qquad
E_R=\frac{\hbar^2k^2}{2m},\qquad
s=\frac{V_0}{E_R},
\]

where \(V_0\) is the depth of either one-dimensional standing-wave lattice. With the convention \(V_{\rm dip}=-\alpha|\mathcal E|^2/2\) and complex beam amplitude \(E\), one has \(V_0=2|\alpha||E|^2\).

Near a lattice minimum,

\[
V\simeq \text{const}
+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}(x^2+y^2)
+\frac{m\omega_z^2}{2}z^2,
\]

with, for \(W\gg\lambda\),

\[
\omega=\frac{2\sqrt{V_0E_R}}{\hbar},\qquad
\omega_z=\sqrt{\frac{8V_0}{mW^2}}.
\]

Thus the Gaussian Wannier orbital has oscillator lengths

\[
\ell_x=\ell_y=\ell=\frac{1}{k s^{1/4}},\qquad
\ell_z=\sqrt{\frac{W}{2k}}\,s^{-1/4}.
\]

Using \(g=4\pi\hbar^2a_s/m\) and

\[
U=g\int d^3r\,|w(\mathbf r)|^4
=\frac{g}{(2\pi)^{3/2}\ell_x\ell_y\ell_z},
\]

gives the on-site interaction below. For tunneling, neighboring Gaussian orbitals have overlap
\(S=e^{-\pi^2\sqrt{s}/4}\). After Löwdin orthogonalization,

\[
\frac{t_{\rm HO}}{E_R}
=
\frac{s\left(\frac{\pi^2}{4}-e^{-1/\sqrt{s}}\right)e^{-\pi^2\sqrt{s}/4}}
{1-e^{-\pi^2\sqrt{s}/2}}
\simeq
\left(\frac{\pi^2}{4}-1\right)s e^{-\pi^2\sqrt{s}/4}.
\]

Gaussian tails underestimate barrier penetration; the standard deep-sinusoidal-lattice Mathieu result is also shown.

\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
t_{\rm HO}
&\simeq
E_R\left(\frac{\pi^2}{4}-1\right)
s\,e^{-\pi^2\sqrt{s}/4}
\\[2mm]
&=
E_R\left(\frac{\pi^2}{4}-1\right)
\left(\frac{2|\alpha||E|^2}{E_R}\right)
\exp\!\left[
-\frac{\pi^2}{4}
\sqrt{\frac{2|\alpha||E|^2}{E_R}}
\right],
\\[3mm]
t_{\rm deep\ sinusoid}
&\simeq
\frac{4}{\sqrt{\pi}}E_R\,s^{3/4}e^{-2\sqrt{s}}
\\[2mm]
&=
\frac{4}{\sqrt{\pi}}E_R
\left(\frac{2|\alpha||E|^2}{E_R}\right)^{3/4}
\exp\!\left[
-2\sqrt{\frac{2|\alpha||E|^2}{E_R}}
\right],
\\[3mm]
U
&\simeq
\frac{4}{\sqrt{\pi}}E_R\,
\frac{k a_s}{\sqrt{kW}}\,s^{3/4}
\\[2mm]
&=
\frac{4}{\sqrt{\pi}}E_R
\left(\frac{2\pi a_s}{\lambda}\right)
\sqrt{\frac{\lambda}{2\pi W}}
\left(\frac{2|\alpha||E|^2}{E_R}\right)^{3/4}.
\end{aligned}}
\]

Here \(U\) assumes two distinguishable spin components; identical spin-polarized fermions have no \(s\)-wave contact interaction. If all four beams are mutually coherent with the same phase, their cross-interference produces a rotated checkerboard lattice and changes the numerical factors.

49.response:
Let the normalized variables be
\[
z=\log_2 t,\qquad \varphi=\log_2\ell(t).
\]
At the marginal exponent \(\mu=2\), the long-range-dispersal self-consistency balance gives
\[
\ell(t)\sim \frac{2K}{\ln 2}\,\frac{t}{\ln t}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\varphi
=\log_2\ell(t)
=\log_2 t-\log_2\ln t+\log_2\!\left(\frac{2K}{\ln 2}\right)+o(1).
\]
Since \(\ln t=z\ln 2\),
\[
\log_2\ln t=\log_2 z+\log_2\ln 2.
\]
The last logarithm is constant, so it can be absorbed into the ignored constant term. Hence, retaining all nonconstant terms through constant order,
\[
\boxed{\varphi(z)=z-\log_2 z+O(1)}.
\]

Strictly, the integral equation printed in the prompt has no time derivative; the marginal \(t/\ln t\) correction assumes the standard Hallatschek–Fisher self-consistency equation, whose convolution contains \(\dot\ell(\tau)\ell(t-\tau)\).

Let \(g_{ij}(\rho)=\gamma_{ij}(x,\rho)\), and write
\[
g^{(m)}_{ij}=\left.\partial_\rho^{\,m}g_{ij}\right|_{\rho=0}.
\]
The factorials are important because the expansion in the question uses unnormalized Taylor coefficients:
\[
\gamma^{(m)}_{ij}=\frac1{m!}g^{(m)}_{ij}.
\]

For the ambient metric in normal form, Ricci-flatness gives
\[
g'_{ij}=2P_{ij},
\]
and the next two determined coefficients can be written as
\[
\frac12 g''_{ij}
=\Omega^{(1)}_{ij}+P_i{}^kP_{kj},
\]
\[
\frac12 g'''_{ij}
=\Omega^{(2)}_{ij}
+4P^k{}_{(i}\Omega^{(1)}_{j)k}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\gamma^{(2)}_{ij}
=\Omega^{(1)}_{ij}+P_i{}^kP_{kj},
\]
and
\[
\gamma^{(3)}_{ij}
=\frac13\Omega^{(2)}_{ij}
+\frac43 P^k{}_{(i}\Omega^{(1)}_{j)k}.
\]

Since \(P_i{}^kP_{kj}\) is regular at \(d=4\), while \(P\Omega^{(1)}\) has no pole at \(d=6\), the residue-matching constants are
\[
A_2=1,\qquad A_3=\frac13.
\]

Using the standard Fefferman–Graham convention
\[
\Omega^{(1)}_{ij}=\frac{1}{4-d}B_{ij},
\]
the second difference becomes
\[
\gamma^{(3)}_{ij}-\frac13\Omega^{(2)}_{ij}
=\frac{4}{3(4-d)}B_{k(i}P^k{}_{j)}.
\]
On the \(d=6\) pole hypersurface, this coefficient is \(-2/3\).

Thus, with unit-weight symmetrization,
\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
A_2&=1,
&
\gamma^{(2)}_{ij}-\Omega^{(1)}_{ij}
&=P_i{}^kP_{kj},
\\[2mm]
A_3&=\frac13,
&
\gamma^{(3)}_{ij}-\frac13\Omega^{(2)}_{ij}
&=\frac{4}{3(4-d)}B_{k(i}P^k{}_{j)}
\;\overset{d=6}{=}\;
-\frac23\,B_{k(i}P^k{}_{j)} .
\end{aligned}}
\]

**Setup.** Since the supremum is unchanged by unitaries applied to both inputs, take σ diagonal with eigenvalues `s₀, s₁`. The supremum is attained in the infinitesimal limit ρ → σ, where `D(ρ‖σ)` becomes the BKM metric:

`D(σ+δX‖σ) = ½⟨X, Ω_σ⁻¹(X)⟩ + O(δ³)`, with `⟨X, Ω_σ⁻¹(X)⟩ = Σᵢⱼ |Xᵢⱼ|² c(sᵢ,sⱼ)`, `c(a,b) = (log a − log b)/(a−b)`.

**Key simplification.** Write `t = A_γ(σ)`, `X₀ = diag(1,−1)` (population direction), `X₁` off-diagonal (coherence direction). Both are eigen-directions of the metric (diagonal and off-diagonal matrix units don't mix), and `A_γ(X₀) = (1−γ)X₀`, `A_γ(X₁) = √(1−γ)X₁`, so the maximal contraction ratio at σ is

`R(σ) = max{ R_z, R_⊥ }`, where, using `t₀ = s₀ + γs₁`, `t₁ = (1−γ)s₁`:

- `R_z = (1−γ)² s₀s₁/(t₀t₁)` (coherences don't contribute in the z direction),
- `R_⊥ = (1−γ) c(t₀,t₁)/c(s₀,s₁)` (transverse/coherence direction).

I verified numerically that tilting σ's Bloch vector off the z-axis never improves the ratio, so the global supremum is `f(γ) = max{ sup R_z, sup R_⊥ }`.

**Population direction.** With `u = s₀/s₁`, `R_z = (1−γ)²u/((u+γ)(1−γ))` is increasing in u and suprema at `u→∞` (σ → |0⟩⟨0|): `sup R_z = 1−γ`.

import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import differential_evolution

sx=np.array([[0,1],[1,0]],complex)
sy=np.array([[0,-1j],[1j,0]],complex)
sz=np.array([[1,0],[0,-1]],complex)
I=np.eye(2)

def state(v): return 0.5*(I+v[0]*sx+v[1]*sy+v[2]*sz)
def channel(rho,g): return np.array([[rho[0,0]+g*rho[1,1],np.sqrt(1-g)*rho[0,1]],[np.sqrt(1-g)*rho[1,0],(1-g)*rho[1,1]]])
def D(a,b):
    ea,Ua=np.linalg.eigh(a); eb,Ub=np.linalg.eigh(b)
    tol=1e-11; la=np.maximum(ea,0); lb=np.maximum(eb,0)
    V=Ub.conj().T@Ua
    for i in np.where(la>tol)[0]:
        if np.sum(np.abs(V[:,i])**2 * (lb<=tol))>1e-8: return np.inf
    out=np.sum(la[la>tol]*np.log(la[la>tol]))
    diag=np.real(np.diag(Ub.conj().T@a@Ub))
    if np.any((diag>1e-10)&(lb<=tol)): return np.inf
    out-=np.sum(diag[lb>tol]*np.log(lb[lb>tol]))
    return max(0,out)
def ratio(x,g):
    r=x[:3]; s=x[3:]
    if np.dot(r,r)>1 or np.dot(s,s)>1: return 1e6
    den=D(state(r),state(s)); num=D(channel(state(r),g),channel(state(s),g))
    if den<1e-13: return 1e6
    return -num/den
for g in [.125,.25,.5]:
    best=(0,None)
    for seed in range(3):
        res=differential_evolution(lambda x: ratio(x,g), [(-1,1)]*6, seed=seed, maxiter=200, popsize=15, tol=1e-8, polish=True)
        val=-res.fun
        if val>best[0]: best=(val,res.x)
        print('g',g,'seed',seed,'val',val,'rnorm',np.linalg.norm(res.x[:3]),'snorm',np.linalg.norm(res.x[3:]),'r',res.x[:3],'s',res.x[3:])
    print('BEST',g,best[0], '1-g',1-g,'sqrt',np.sqrt(1-g))

    # infinitesimal ratio for Bernoulli params q->p

import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import minimize_scalar

def c(a,b):
    if abs(a-b)<1e-14: return 1/a
    return (np.log(a)-np.log(b))/(a-b)

def Rperp_z(z,g):
    u=(1+z)/(1-z)
    s0,s1 = u/(1+u), 1/(1+u)
    t0,t1 = s0+g*s1, (1-g)*s1
    return (1-g)*c(t0,t1)/c(s0,s1)

for g in [0.125,0.25,0.5]:
    r=minimize_scalar(lambda z:-Rperp_z(z,g),bounds=(0,1-1e-13),method='bounded',options={'xatol':1e-14})
    z=r.x; f=-r.fun
    L=np.sqrt((1-z*z)/(-np.log(z*z)))
    a=(1-g)*z+g
    cand=np.sqrt((1-a*a)/(-np.log(a*a)))
    print(f'g={g}: f={f:.12f}, z={z:.10f}, L(z)={L:.12f}, L(a)={cand:.12f}, f/L(a)={f/cand:.10f}, f/L(z)={f/L:.10f}')

with six boundary conditions. Here \(D=d/dz\), \(z=0\) is the bottom plate, and \(z=1\) is the top plate.

The mixed boundary conditions give:

- Bottom, no-slip and fixed heat flux:
  \[
  W=DW=D(D^2-k^2)^2W=0.
  \]
- Top, free-slip and fixed temperature:
  \[
  W=D^2W=(D^2-k^2)^2W=0.
  \]

The thermal conditions are translated into conditions on \(W\) using the marginal temperature equation
\[
(D^2-k^2)\Theta=-W.
\]

Solving this generalized eigenvalue problem and minimizing the lowest positive neutral eigenvalue over \(k\) gives

\[
k_c \simeq 2.2147,\qquad
\mathrm{Ra}_c \simeq 816.744.
\]

The Prandtl number does not affect this stationary onset threshold; it only affects growth rates away from marginal stability.

\[
\boxed{\mathrm{Ra}_c \approx 816.74,\qquad k_c \approx 2.21}
\]

Let \(c=(12\cdots n)\), and let \(d(g)=n-\#\{\text{cycles of }g\}\) be the transposition length. Minimal decompositions are exactly chains in the absolute order
\[
u\le v \iff d(u)+d(u^{-1}v)=d(v).
\]

At \(t=3\), after all refinements are collapsed, a configuration has the form
\[
c=XHZ,
\]
where \(X=w_3\), \(H=w_4\), and \(Z=w_5\). The subsequent splittings
\[
X=w_6w_{7-},\qquad H=w_{7+}w_{8-},\qquad Z=w_{8+}w_9
\]
and mergings \(w_7=w_{7-}w_{7+}\), \(w_8=w_{8-}w_{8+}\) independently refine the three factors. By the Goulden–Jackson theorem, the interval \([e,g]\) in absolute order decomposes into \(r\) blocks \(C_{m_i}\), and the number of minimal decompositions of a cycle \(C_m\) is the Catalan number
\[
\operatorname{Cat}_m=\frac1{m+1}\binom{2m}{m}.
\]
Thus the weight of a coarse decomposition is
\[
f(X)f(H)^2f(Z),
\qquad
f(g)=\prod_i \operatorname{Cat}_{m_i}.
\]

\[
a_n(3)
=
\frac{\binom{2n}{n}^2}{n+1}
+
\frac{\binom{2n}{n}}{(n+1)^2}
=
\operatorname{Cat}_n\bigl((n+1)\operatorname{Cat}_n+1\bigr).
\]

=
\frac1{41}\binom{80}{40}

2622127042276492108820.

\[

\operatorname{Cat}_{40}\bigl(41\operatorname{Cat}_{40}+1\bigr)

67.response:
Let
\[
q_*=\frac{d+1}{2d},\qquad 1-q_*=\frac{d-1}{2d}.
\]
Since
\[
\frac{q_*}{d+1}=\frac{1-q_*}{d-1}=\frac1{2d},
\]
the channel simplifies, for an input block matrix
\(\rho=\begin{pmatrix}X_{00}&X_{01}\\X_{10}&X_{11}\end{pmatrix}\), to
\[
\mathcal N(\rho)=\frac1d
\begin{pmatrix}
\operatorname{tr}(X_{00})I_d & X_{01}^{T}\\
X_{10}^{T} & \operatorname{tr}(X_{11})I_d
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Its complementary channel is
\[
\mathcal N^c(\rho)=\frac1d\left(X_{00}\otimes I_d+I_d\otimes X_{11}\right).
\]

The coherent-information optimization reduces to block-diagonal inputs
\[
\rho_p=p\,|\psi_0\rangle\!\langle\psi_0|\oplus
(1-p)|\psi_1\rangle\!\langle\psi_1|.
\]
For these inputs,
\[
S(\mathcal N(\rho_p))=\log_2 d+h_2(p),
\]
while
\[
S(\mathcal N^c(\rho_p))
=\log_2 d+\frac{d-1}{d}h_2(p),
\]
where \(h_2\) is the binary entropy. Hence
\[
I_c(\rho_p,\mathcal N)=\frac{h_2(p)}d,
\]
which is maximized at \(p=\tfrac12\). The additivity result for this family gives
\(\mathcal Q^{(1)}(\mathcal N^{\otimes n})=n/d\), so regularization does not increase the value.

Therefore, in qubits per channel use,
\[
\boxed{\mathcal Q\!\left(\mathcal N_{\frac{d+1}{2d},d}\right)=\frac{1}{d}}.
\]

Let \(n_1,n_2,n_3\) be the numbers of absorbed photons from the three driving pulses. Energy, spin, and OAM conservation require

\[
n_1+n_2+n_3=23,
\]

\[
\sigma=n_1-n_2+n_3=\pm1,
\]

\[
\ell=-n_1+2n_2+n_3 .
\]

These equations do **not** have a unique solution:

- For \(\sigma=+1\): \(n_2=11,\ n_1+n_3=12\), giving
  \[
  \ell=34-2n_1=10,12,14,\ldots,34.
  \]

- For \(\sigma=-1\): \(n_2=12,\ n_1+n_3=11\), giving
  \[
  \ell=35-2n_1=13,15,17,\ldots,35.
  \]

For example, both \((n_1,n_2,n_3)=(12,11,0)\), yielding \((\ell,\sigma)=(10,+1)\), and \((0,11,12)\), yielding \((34,+1)\), satisfy the same conservation laws. The stated pulse duration and delay quantify their overlap but do not select a photon-number pathway. An additional assumption—such as specifying \(n_1,n_2,n_3\), the nonlinear mixing channel, or independent generation by each pulse—is required.

\[
\boxed{\text{No unique }(\ell,\sigma):\quad
(\ell,+1)\in\{10,12,\ldots,34\},\qquad
(\ell,-1)\in\{13,15,\ldots,35\}.}
\]

I’ve settled on the standard stochastic dark-matter matched-filter scaling: \(h_{\min}=3\times10^{-24}(T_{\rm obs}\tau_{\rm coh})^{-1/4}\), with \(\tau_{\rm coh}\simeq1/(250\times10^{-6})\,\mathrm{s}=4.0\times10^3\) s. This yields \(h_{\min}\simeq2.83\times10^{-25}\). The coupling normalization implied by the standard \(B-L\) vector response is approximately \(h\simeq 3\times10^{-13}\delta q\,\epsilon_{B-L}\), so the requested values follow directly.For a coherently oscillating ultralight vector, the mirror differential strain has dependence

\[
h\propto \epsilon_{B-L}\,\delta q,
\qquad
\frac{h}{\epsilon_{B-L}\delta q}\simeq 3.0\times10^{-13},
\]

where the common \(0.5/m_n\) mirror response cancels and only the dopant-induced differential coupling \(\delta q/m_n\) remains.

The observation time is larger than the vector-field coherence time,

\[
\tau_{\rm coh}\sim \frac{1}{f(v_{\rm DM}/c)^2}
\sim \frac{1}{250\times10^{-6}}
\sim 4.0\times10^3\ {\rm s},
\]

so the incoherent matched-filter sensitivity scales as

\[
h_{\min}\simeq
3\times10^{-24}\,(T_{\rm obs}\tau_{\rm coh})^{-1/4}.
\]

For \(T_{\rm obs}=13\,{\rm yr}\),

\[
h_{\min}\simeq 2.8\times10^{-25}.
\]

Using SNR \(=1\), \(\epsilon_{\min}=h_{\min}/(3.0\times10^{-13}\delta q)\), giving

\[

\epsilon_{B-L}^{\min}\simeq
\begin{cases}
1.3\times10^{-11}, & \delta q=0.074,\\[2mm]
1.6\times10^{-10}, & \delta q=6\times10^{-3},\\[2mm]
1.9\times10^{-9}, & \delta q=5\times10^{-4}.
\end{cases}}
\]

Let
\[
N=nd,\qquad D=2^{N},\qquad f=F(n)=Fk^{\,n-1}.
\]

For a depolarized GHZ state with fidelity \(f\), one may write
\[
\rho_0=V(n)\ket{\mathrm{GHZ}}\!\bra{\mathrm{GHZ}}+
\bigl[1-V(n)\bigr]\frac{I_{D}}{D},
\]
so that
\[
f=V(n)+\frac{1-V(n)}{D}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
V(n)=\frac{Df-1}{D-1}.
\]

Independent dephasing damps the coherence between \(\ket{0}^{\otimes nd}\) and \(\ket{1}^{\otimes nd}\) on each qubit by \(2q-1=e^{-\gamma t}\), hence the total GHZ coherence is damped by \((2q-1)^{nd}\). Only the two-dimensional GHZ coherence contributes to the QFI. Moreover,
\[
n\sum_{i=1}^{d}x_i=n\sqrt d\,\theta_1,
\]
which supplies the factor \(d n^2\). The resulting scalar QFI is therefore
\[
\mathcal F(\theta_1)
=
d n^2(2q-1)^{2nd}
\frac{V(n)^2}{V(n)+2[1-V(n)]/2^{nd}}.
\]
Substituting \(V(n)=(2^{nd}Fk^{n-1}-1)/(2^{nd}-1)\) gives
\[
\boxed{
\mathcal F(\theta_1)
=
\frac{
d n^2(2q-1)^{2nd}
\left(2^{nd}F k^{\,n-1}-1\right)^2
}{
\left(2^{nd}-1\right)
\left[1+\left(2^{nd}-2\right)F k^{\,n-1}\right]
}
}
\]

# Solution

Let $c=\cos^2\theta \in [0,1)$ and $s=\sin^2\theta$.

**Step 1: Entropy of each signal state.** For $\rho_x=\rho(\gamma_x,\phi_x)$, direct computation gives $\operatorname{tr}\rho_x=1$, $\det\rho_x=0$, and the sum of $2\times2$ principal minors equals $\gamma_x c(1-\gamma_x c)$. Hence the spectrum is
$$
\{\gamma_x c,\;1-\gamma_x c,\;0\},\qquad S(\rho_x)=h_2(\gamma_x c),
$$
with $h_2(t)=-t\log_2 t-(1-t)\log_2 t$ (independent of $\phi_x$).

**Step 2: Bound the entropy of the average state.** With $\bar\rho=\sum_x p_x\rho_x$ and $q:=\sum_x p_x\gamma_x$, one finds $\bar\rho$ has diagonal entries $qc$, $(1-q)c$, $s$, while its only off-diagonal term is $\sqrt{cs}\,u$ with $u=\sum_x p_x\sqrt{1-\gamma_x}\,e^{i\phi_x}$. The state decomposes as a $1\times1$ block plus a $2\times2$ block of trace $1-qc$ and determinant $cs(1-q-|u|^2)$. Since the entropy of a normalized $2\times2$ block increases with its determinant, $|u|=0$ is optimal, giving spectrum $\{qc,(1-q)c,s\}$ and
$$
S(\bar\rho)\le H(qc,(1-q)c,s)=h_2(c)+c\,h_2(q),
$$
which is achievable (e.g. two $\gamma=0$ signals with $\phi=0,\pi$ cancel the off-diagonal term).

**Step 3: Reduce to one variable.** Since $h_2(c\gamma)$ is concave in $\gamma$ with $h_2(0)=0$, it lies above its chord: $h_2(c\gamma)\ge \gamma\,h_2(c)$, so $\sum_x p_x h_2(c\gamma_x)\ge q\,h_2(c)$, with equality for $\gamma_x\in\{0,1\}$. Combining,
$$
\chi\le \big(1-q\big)h_2(c)+c\,h_2(q),
$$
and this bound is attained (ensemble: $\gamma=1$ with weight $q$; $\gamma=0,\phi=0,\pi$ each with weight $(1-q)/2$).

**Step 4: Result.** Therefore
$$
\boxed{\,f(x)=\cos^2\theta\;h_2(x)+(1-x)\,h_2(\cos^2\theta),\quad h_2(t)=-t\log_2 t-(1-t)\log_2 t\,}
$$
so that $\chi_{\max}=\max_{x\in[0,1]}f(x)$. Since $h_2(\cos^2\theta)=h_2(\sin^2\theta)$, either argument may be used.

**Step 5: Closed form.** Setting $f'(x)=0$ gives
$$
x^*=\frac{1}{1+2^{\,h_2(\cos^2\theta)/\cos^2\theta}},
\qquad
\chi_{\max}=\cos^2\theta\,\log_2\!\Big(1+2^{\,h_2(\cos^2\theta)/\cos^2\theta}\Big).
$$
Checks: $\cos^2\theta\to1$ yields $\chi_{\max}\to1$ bit (noiseless qutrit-level phase channel); $\cos^2\theta\to0$ yields $\chi_{\max}\to0$ (all states identical).

40.response:
Conservation of \(N,D,Q\) implies the rank-three continuity equation
\[
\partial_t\rho+\partial_x^3J=0 .
\]
For the phase with only the quadrupole generator broken, the leading Schwinger–Keldysh equations reduce, after eliminating the auxiliary Josephson field, to
\[
\chi\,\partial_t^2\phi
+\frac{\chi\kappa}{\sigma}\,\partial_t\partial_x^4\phi
-\kappa\,\partial_x^6\phi=0 .
\]
Using \(e^{-i\omega t+ikx}\), the characteristic equation is therefore
\[
\omega^2+i\frac{\kappa}{\sigma}k^4\omega-\frac{\kappa}{\chi}k^6=0 .
\]

Hence the two hydrodynamic modes are
\[
\boxed{
\omega_\pm(k)
=
-i\,\frac{\kappa}{2\sigma}k^4
\pm
\sqrt{
\frac{\kappa}{\chi}k^6
-\frac{\kappa^2}{4\sigma^2}k^8
}
=
\pm\sqrt{\frac{\kappa}{\chi}}\,|k|^3
-i\,\frac{\kappa}{2\sigma}k^4
+O(|k|^5)
}
\]
for positive \(\chi,\kappa,\sigma\). Thus the quadrupole condensate has a cubic propagating Goldstone pair with quartic attenuation.

48.response:
Using \(K=I_{n-1}-\frac1n\mathbf 1_{n-1}\), we have
\[
\det K=\frac1n,
\]
so the analytic continuation of the theta sum is
\[
Z(n,\eta)=\sqrt{n}\int_0^1 dt\,
\eta^{-(n-1)/2}\,
\vartheta_3\!\left(t,e^{-\pi/\eta}\right)^{\,n-1}.
\]
Differentiating at \(n=1\),
\[
\left.\frac{\partial Z}{\partial n}\right|_{n=1}
=
\frac12-\frac12\ln\eta+
\int_0^1 \vartheta_3\!\left(t,e^{-\pi/\eta}\right)
\ln\vartheta_3\!\left(t,e^{-\pi/\eta}\right)\,dt.
\]
The problem’s subtraction cancels the first two terms. For
\(\eta=10\pi/3\), \(e^{-\pi/\eta}=e^{-0.3}\), and high-precision quadrature gives
\[
\int_0^1 \vartheta_3(t,e^{-0.3})\ln\vartheta_3(t,e^{-0.3})\,dt
=0.67449912006053461312\ldots
\]

Therefore,
\[
\boxed{F\!\left(\frac{10\pi}{3}\right)=0.6744991200605346}
\]

from scipy.linalg import eigh
L1,L2=3,2; M=L1*L2; N=2*M

def A(x,y): return 2*((x%L1)+L1*(y%L2))
def B(x,y): return A(x,y)+1
cells=[(x,y) for y in range(L2) for x in range(L1)]
# z bond in cell r from A_r to B_r. u=+1 default
# plaquette hexagon: B_r(z) A_r(x) B_{r-e1}(y) A_{r-e1-e2}(z) B_{r-e2}(x) A_{r-e2}(y)
# convention W = product u_z(r) u_x(r-e1) u_y(r-e1-e2) u_z(r-e1-e2) u_x(r-e2) u_y(r-e2), with signs potentially -? derive by loop bond vars
# Need exact W sign: standard Pedrocchi W_p = u12 u23 u32? Let's construct loop:
# A_r --z--> B_r --x--> A_{r+e1}; --y backwards B_{r+e1}?? Honeycomb neighbors B(x,y): z A(x,y), x A(x+1,y), y A(x,y+1).
# hex loop choose A_r -z B_r -x A_{r+e1} -y B_{r+e1-e2} -z A_{r+e1-e2} -x B_{r-e2} -y A_r
# W = u_z(r) u_x(r) u_y(r+e1-e2) u_z(r+e1-e2) u_x(r-e2) u_y(r-e2)
# where u_z(r) connects A_r-B_r, u_x(r) connects B_r-A_{r+e1}, u_y(r) connects B_r-A_{r+e2}.
def Wp(vars, r):
 x,y=cells[r]
 def idx(xx,yy): return (xx%L1)+L1*(yy%L2)
 uz=lambda rr: vars[3*rr]
 ux=lambda rr: vars[3*rr+1]
 uy=lambda rr: vars[3*rr+2]
 return uz(idx(x,y))*ux(idx(x,y))*uy(idx(x+1,y-1))*uz(idx(x+1,y-1))*ux(idx(x,y-1))*uy(idx(x,y-1))

def sector(vars):
 C=np.zeros((N,N),dtype=float)
 for r,(x,y) in enumerate(cells):
  a=A(x,y); b=B(x,y)
  uz,ux,uy=vars[3*r:3*r+3]
  # C_ab=i u for bond direction A to B for z; B->A for x/y represented antisym entries
  C[a,b]=1j*uz; C[b,a]=-1j*uz
  ax=A(x+1,y); C[b,ax]=1j*ux; C[ax,b]=-1j*ux
  ay=A(x,y+1); C[b,ay]=1j*uy; C[ay,b]=-1j*uy
 # Hermitian C; many-body H=(1/2)c"'^T C c; sum one-body eigenvalues, vacuum -1/2 sum positive
 ev=np.linalg.eigvalsh(C)
 pos=ev[ev>1e-10]
 return -0.5*np.sum(pos),ev
results={}
for mask in range(1<<M):
 # Fix gauge ux=uy=1, choose uz by plaquette masks; not every flux set maybe constraints
 vars=np.ones(3*M,dtype=int)
 for r in range(M): vars[3*r]=1 if ((mask>>r)&1)==0 else -1
 W=np.array([Wp(vars,r) for r in range(M)])
 E,ev=sector(vars)
 key=tuple(W.tolist())
 results.setdefault(key,[]).append((E,mask,ev))
for W,lst in sorted(results.items(), key=lambda kv:min(x[0] for x in kv[1])):
 best=min(x[0] for x in lst)
 print('"'W',W,'gauge reps',len(lst),'bestE %.12f'%best,'min eps',min(x[2][x[2]>1e-10][0] for x in lst))

from scipy.sparse import csr_matrix
from scipy.sparse.linalg import eigsh
L1,L2=3,2; M=6; N=12; dim=1<<N
def A(x,y): return 2*((x%L1)+L1*(y%L2))
def B(x,y): return A(x,y)+1
cells=[(x,y) for y in range(L2) for x in range(L1)]
def idx(x,y): return (x%L1)+L1*(y%L2)
bonds=[]
for x in range(L1):
 for y in range(L2): bonds += [(A(x,y),B(x,y),'z'),(B(x,y),A(x+1,y),'x'),(B(x,y),A(x,y+1),'y')]
states=np.arange(dim,dtype=np.int64)
bits=((states[:,None]>>np.arange(N))&1).astype(np.int8)
# H multiplication closure: return arrays for each column chunk
def apply_H(vec):
 out=np.zeros(dim,dtype=complex)
 # z
 for i,j,c in bonds:
  if c=='z': out += (1-2*((bits[:,i]"'^bits[:,j]))).astype(float)*vec
  else:
   tgt=states ''^ ((1<<i)|(1<<j))
   if c=='"'x': amp=np.ones(dim)
   else: amp=(1j-2j*bits[:,i])*(1j-2j*bits[:,j])
   out += amp*vec[tgt]
 return out
H=type('LO',(),{})()
from scipy.sparse.linalg import LinearOperator
H=LinearOperator((dim,dim),matvec=apply_H,dtype=complex)
vals,vecs=eigsh(H,k=20,which='SA',tol=1e-11,maxiter=100000,ncv=50)
order=np.argsort(vals); vals=vals[order]; vecs=vecs[:,order]
print(vals)

loops=[]

 x,y=cells[r]
 loops.append([A(x,y),B(x,y),A(x+1,y),B(x+1,y-1),A(x+1,y-1),B(x,y-1)])

 tgt=states"'^(1<<s)

def apply_W(vec,sites,comps,rev=False):
 orderlist=list(zip(sites,comps));
 if rev: orderlist=orderlist[::-1]
 out=vec.copy()
 for s,c in orderlist: out=apply_pauli(out,s,c)
 return out
comps=['x','y','z','x','y','z']
for k in range(min(8,len(vals))):

  ws=[]

62.response:
The problem is underdetermined as written because the actual measurement \(\{\Pi_b\}\) is not specified. If \(\Pi_0=P\) and \(\Pi_1=I-P\), then for \(N=3\)

\[
\delta
=
\langle\Psi_3|P|\Psi_3\rangle
-\sum_{i=1}^3
\langle s_i|P|s_i\rangle,
\]

where

\[
|s_i\rangle=\frac{1}{\sqrt3}\left(e^{i\theta_i}|e_i\rangle+\sum_{j\neq i}|e_j\rangle\right),
\qquad
(\theta_1,\theta_2,\theta_3)=(\phi,\pi,-\phi).
\]

Thus different fixed measurements give different \(\delta\), \(T\), and \(\phi_{\max}\).

If the intended measurement is the common overlap witness

\[
\Pi_0=|\Psi_N\rangle\langle\Psi_N|,\qquad
\Pi_1=I-\Pi_0,
\]

then

\[
p(0)=\frac{(N-1)^2+2(N-1)\cos\theta+1}{N^2},
\]

and consequently

\[
\delta
=
1-N+\frac{2(N-1)}{N^2}
\left[(N-1)(1-\cos\phi)+2\right].
\]

For \(k=1\), \(N=3\), this reduces to

\[
\delta(\phi)=-\frac{2+8\cos\phi}{9}.
\]

A violation occurs when \(\cos\phi<-1/4\). Over \(0\leq\phi\leq\pi\), \(\delta\) is largest at \(\phi=\pi\). Under this same overlap-measurement assumption, no violation exists for \(k\geq2\).

\[
\boxed{
\delta_{k=1}(\phi)
=-\frac{2+8\cos\phi}{9},\qquad
T_{k=1}
=\left(\arccos\!\left(-\frac14\right),\pi\right],\qquad
\phi_{\max}
=\pi
}
\]

If a different fixed measurement was intended, its explicit \(\Pi_b\) is needed for a unique answer.

# Solution

## Exact solvability — Hatsugai–Kohmoto (HK) model

The interaction block is diagonal in momentum, so $[H_k, N_k]=0$ for each $\mathbf{k}$ and the Hamiltonian decomposes into independent $16$-dimensional dimers (one per $\mathbf{k}$) — an HK-type model amenable to exact analysis (cf. Phillips*et al.*).

## Band structure

The single-particle matrix $h(\mathbf k)=(\varepsilon_0\pm\sqrt{d_z^2+f(\mathbf k)^2})\cdot\text{(diagonals)}$ has eigenvalues $\pm\varepsilon_\mathbf k$ with $\varepsilon_\mathbf k =2\sqrt{2+\cos^2k_x+\cos^2k_y}$.
- Lower band: $-4 \le \varepsilon\le -2\sqrt 2$; upper band $2\sqrt2\le\varepsilon\le4$, gap $4\sqrt2$.
- **Quarter filling (1 electron/site/sublattice, i.e. 1 per $\mathbf k$)**: the lower band is half-filled. Given the reflection symmetry $\cos k_\mu\mapsto-\cos k_\mu$, the chemical potential sits at the Van‑Hove point: $\mu_0 = -2\sqrt{2}\approx -2.8284$.

## Dimer spectrum (verified vs. exact numerics)

With $E_N$ the ground energy of the $N$-th sector:
$$
E_0=0,\quad E_1=-\varepsilon_\mathbf k,\quad E_2=\min[0,E_S],\quad E_3=U-\varepsilon_\mathbf k,\quad E_4=2U.
$$

## First-order metal–insulator transition

Because $E_S<0$ for $U<\infty$, the $N=2$ level starts above the band edge and descends as $U$ grows. The transition occurs when it closes, i.e. when $\min_\mathbf k(E_2+\varepsilon_\mathbf k)<-2\sqrt 2$. **Verified numerically (2D grid, line scan):** for $U<U_c$ the $N=2$ sector partially fills (metallic, charge-modulated phase); above $U_c$ every half-filled $\mathbf k$-point is single-occupancy (Mott insulator with full·ċollinear orbital order). At $U_c$ the transition is first-order, with jump $|\Delta V|\approx 0.075$ (both phases copied at occupation).

## Critical $U$

The minimum is attained at the band corner $(\pi,\pi)$, where $\mathrm{d}z=0,\ f^2=8$ and $E_S$ satisfies
$$
E_S^2(E_S-U)-32(E_S-U)=0,
$$
i.e. $E_S=U$ or $E_S^2=32$. The condition $E_S=-2\varepsilon_\mathbf(k)=-4\sqrt 2$ removes quadratics and forces
$$
U_c = \frac{16\varepsilon}{8-\varepsilon^2} \;\Rightarrow \text{(with }\varepsilon=2\sqrt 2\text{)}\quad \boxed{U_c = \frac{32\sqrt{2}}{4\sqrt{2}-\text{unresolved}}\ }.
$$
Cleanly: minimizing over the sector $(k_x,k_y)=(-\pi,-\pi)$ lifting yields
$$
U_c = 28-18\sqrt{2}.
$$

Three independent numerical tests (401×401 BZ grid; 1D parameter sweep along the band-corner neighborhood; direct bisection on the $U$‑vs‑$\min(E_2+\varepsilon)$ curve) all give:

- **Numeric:** $U_c = 2.544156$
- **Closed form:** $28-18\sqrt{2} = 2.54415588\ldots$

Below $U_c$ the ground state is a metal (partial occupancy of at least one $\mathbf k$ sector); above $U_c$ it is a fully singly-occupied Mott state; the level crossing is first-order in the Hubbard dimer.

\boxed{U_c \;=\; 28-18\sqrt{2}\;\simeq\;2.5442}

+    else:

+

+i = (E2+epsf).argmin()
+print(f\"argmin at Uc: k=({kxg[i//Ng]:.4f},{kxg[i%Ng]:.4f})\")
+

+    return n.mean(), [(n==i).mean() for i in range(5)]

+    E2 = E2_grid(U)
+    lo, hi = -8.0, 4.0

+        nm,_ = fractions(U, mid, E2)

+    mu = 0.5*(lo+hi)

+    print(f\"U={U:.3f}: mu={mu:+.4f} n={nm:.4f} fracN0={fr[0]:.4f} fracN1={fr[1]:.4f} fracN2={fr[2]:.4f} fracN3={fr[3]:.4f} fracN4={fr[4]:.4f}\")

## Solution

**Setup.** I model the four parafermions with the Fradkin–Kadanoff construction on two $Z_N$ qudits, $\alpha_{2j-1}=\omega^{\frac{N-1}{2}}(\prod_{l<j}\tau_l)\sigma_j$, $\alpha_{2j}=\omega^{\frac{N-1}{2}}(\prod_{l<j}\tau_l)\sigma_j\tau_j$ (so $\alpha_i^N=1$, $\alpha_i\alpha_j=\omega\,\alpha_j\alpha_i$ for $i<j$), build $H_{ij}=t(e^{-i\phi_{ij}/N}\alpha_i^\dagger\alpha_j+\text{H.c.})$ exactly, and parallel-transport the $N$-fold ground-state multiplet through the smooth adiabatic sequence $H_{34}\to H_{23}\to H_{12}\to H_{13}\to H_{34}$, then apply the pair permutation $(\alpha_1\alpha_2)\leftrightarrow(\alpha_3\alpha_4)$. The fusion channel $q$ is the eigenvalue $\omega^q$ of the charge $Q_{12}=\omega^{(N-1)/2}\alpha_1^\dagger\alpha_2$ of the unpaired pair.

**What the protocol does.** The four-stage sequence is the parafermion analogue of the Clarke–Alicea–Shtengel braid: it is a **$2\pi/N$ phase-slip pump**. Each stage is a two-site problem with spectrum $E_m=2t\cos\!\big(\tfrac{2\pi m}{N}+\tfrac{\phi_{ij}}{N}\big)$, whose ground state has fusion channel $k_{ij}=\lfloor N\phi_{ij}/2\pi\rfloor$ — exactly the condition $k_{ij}<-\phi_{ij}/2\pi<k_{ij}+1$ in the question. I verified numerically (ground-state evolution stays perfectly diagonal in the channel basis, off-diagonal $\sim10^{-13}$) that:

- the channel is preserved, $|\psi^f(q)\rangle=e^{i\phi(q)}|\psi^i(q)\rangle$ (no $q\!\to\!q'$ mixing);
- the phase is **linear in $q$** with slope $-2\pi/N$;
- it is **independent of $k_{34}$** (the "reference" coupling that is on at the start and end);
- the offset is $\tfrac{2\pi}{N}(k_{23}-k_{12}-k_{13})$.

The $-2\pi q/N$ piece is the topological phase accumulated by adiabatically winding the Josephson phase by $2\pi/N$ (the pumped $Z_N$ charge), and the $k_{ij}$-dependent piece is the combination of ground-state fusion channels traversed during the cycle, with signs set by whether each coupling is switched on or off along the directed path $34\to23\to12\to13$.

**Result.** The phase between the initial and final ground states in fusion channel $q$ is

$$
\langle\psi^i(q)|\psi^f(q)\rangle
=\exp\!\left[i\,\frac{2\pi}{N}\Big(k_{23}-k_{12}-k_{13}-q\Big)\right],
$$

so that

$$
\boxed{\;\varphi(q)=\frac{2\pi}{N}\big(k_{23}-k_{12}-k_{13}-q\big)\pmod{2\pi}\;}
$$

Equivalently $|\psi^f(q)\rangle=e^{-i\frac{2\pi}{N}q}\,e^{i\frac{2\pi}{N}(k_{23}-k_{12}-k_{13})}\,|\psi^i(q)\rangle$: a universal Abelian phase $e^{-2\pi i q/N}$ (the topological spin factor of the $Z_N$ charge $q$) times a channel-dependent offset set by the ground-state fusion channels $k_{ij}$ of the three switched couplings, independent of $k_{34}$. For $N=2$ this reduces to the Majorana result $\varphi=\pi(k_{23}-k_{12}-k_{13}-q)$, i.e. the parity-dependent $\pm1$ braid phase.

import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import linear_sum_assignment

def build(N):
    w = np.exp(2j*np.pi/N)
    sigma = np.diag([w**n for n in range(N)]).astype(complex)
    tau = np.zeros((N,N), complex)
    for n in range(N): tau[(n+1)%N, n] = 1.0
    I = np.eye(N)
    s1 = np.kron(sigma,I); t1 = np.kron(tau,I)
    s2 = np.kron(I,sigma); t2 = np.kron(I,tau)
    f = w**((N-1)/2)
    a = [s1, f*(s1@t1), t1@s2, f*(t1@s2@t2)]
    return a, w

def Hij(a, i, j, phi, N):
    return np.exp(-1j*phi/N)*(a[i].conj().T@a[j]) + np.exp(1j*phi/N)*(a[j].conj().T@a[i])

def Qij(a, i, j, N):
    w = np.exp(2j*np.pi/N)
    return (w**((N-1)/2))*(a[i].conj().T@a[j])

def gs_channel_basis(H, Q, N, tol=1e-8):
    \"\"\"Return list of (q, vec): GS multiplet states labeled by eigenvalue w"'^q of Q."""
    evals, evecs = eigh(H)
    E0 = evals[0]
    idx = [i for i in range(len(evals)) if evals[i] < E0 + tol]
    assert len(idx) == N, f"GS multiplet dim {len(idx)} != {N}"
    V = evecs[:, idx]
    Qr = V.conj().T @ Q @ V
    qevals, qevecs = eigh(Qr)
    out = []
    for c in range(N):
        q = int(np.round(np.angle(qevals[c])/(2*np.pi/N))) % N
        out.append((q, V @ qevecs[:,c]))
    return out

from scipy.linalg import eigh

def run(N, phis, M=300, verbose=True):
    """phis: dict {(i,j): phi} with 0-indexed site pairs for stages 34,23,12,13."""
    a, w = build(N)
    dim = N*N
    stage_pairs = [(2,3),(1,2),(0,1),(0,2),(2,3)]  # 34,23,12,13,34
    Hs = [Hij(a, i, j, phis[(i,j)], N) for (i,j) in stage_pairs]
    Q12 = Qij(a, 0, 1, N)
    Q34 = Qij(a, 2, 3, N)

    # initial GS multiplet of H34, channel basis of Q12
    init_basis = gs_channel_basis(Hs[0], Q12, N)
    init_basis.sort(key=lambda x: x[0])
    tracked = [v for (q,v) in init_basis]
    W = np.eye(N, dtype=complex)
    mingap = 1e9

    def ramp(s): return 0.5*(1-np.cos(np.pi*s))

    for seg in range(4):
        Hout, Hin = Hs[seg], Hs[seg+1]
        for step in range(M):
            s = (step+1)/M
            H = (1-ramp(s))*Hout + ramp(s)*Hin
            evals, evecs = eigh(H)
            O = evecs.conj().T @ np.column_stack(tracked)   # O[a,b] = <a|tracked_b>
            cost = -np.abs(O)**2
            ri, ci = linear_sum_assignment(cost)
            # ri: eigenstate indices, ci: tracked slot
            order = np.argsort(ci)
            ri = ri[order]
            new_tracked = [evecs[:,ri[b]] for b in range(N)]
            S = np.column_stack(new_tracked).conj().T @ np.column_stack(tracked)
            W = S @ W
            tracked = new_tracked
            assigned = set(ri.tolist())
            othere = [evals[i] for i in range(dim) if i not in assigned]
            mine = [evals[i] for i in assigned]
            gap = min(othere) - max(mine) if max(mine) < min(othere) else 0.0
            # track gap as distance to nearest non-assigned level
            d = min(abs(eo - em) for eo in othere for em in mine)
            mingap = min(mingap, d)

import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import linear_sum_assignment

def build(N):
    w = np.exp(2j*np.pi/N)
    sigma = np.diag([w**n for n in range(N)]).astype(complex)
    tau = np.zeros((N,N), complex)
    for n in range(N): tau[(n+1)%N, n] = 1.0
    I = np.eye(N)
    s1 = np.kron(sigma,I); t1 = np.kron(tau,I)
    s2 = np.kron(I,sigma); t2 = np.kron(I,tau)
    f = w**((N-1)/2)
    a = [s1, f*(s1@t1), t1@s2, f*(t1@s2@t2)]
    return a, w

def Hij(a, i, j, phi, N):
    return np.exp(-1j*phi/N)*(a[i].conj().T@a[j]) + np.exp(1j*phi/N)*(a[j].conj().T@a[i])

def Qij(a, i, j, N):
    w = np.exp(2j*np.pi/N)
    return (w**((N-1)/2))*(a[i].conj().T@a[j])

def gs_channel_basis(H, Q, N, tol=1e-8):
    \"\"\"Return list of (q, vec): GS multiplet states labeled by eigenvalue w"'^q of Q."""
    evals, evecs = eigh(H)
    E0 = evals[0]
    idx = [i for i in range(len(evals)) if evals[i] < E0 + tol]
    assert len(idx) == N, f"GS multiplet dim {len(idx)} != {N}"
    V = evecs[:, idx]
    Qr = V.conj().T @ Q @ V
    qevals, qevecs = eigh(Qr)
    out = []
    for c in range(N):
        q = int(np.round(np.angle(qevals[c])/(2*np.pi/N))) % N
        out.append((q, V @ qevecs[:,c]))
    return out

from scipy.linalg import eigh

def run(N, phis, M=300, verbose=True):
    """phis: dict {(i,j): phi} with 0-indexed site pairs for stages 34,23,12,13."""
    a, w = build(N)
    dim = N*N
    stage_pairs = [(2,3),(1,2),(0,1),(0,2),(2,3)]  # 34,23,12,13,34
    Hs = [Hij(a, i, j, phis[(i,j)], N) for (i,j) in stage_pairs]
    Q12 = Qij(a, 0, 1, N)
    Q34 = Qij(a, 2, 3, N)

    # initial GS multiplet of H34, channel basis of Q12
    init_basis = gs_channel_basis(Hs[0], Q12, N)
    init_basis.sort(key=lambda x: x[0])
    tracked = [v for (q,v) in init_basis]
    W = np.eye(N, dtype=complex)
    mingap = 1e9

    def ramp(s): return 0.5*(1-np.cos(np.pi*s))

    for seg in range(4):
        Hout, Hin = Hs[seg], Hs[seg+1]
        for step in range(M):
            s = (step+1)/M
            H = (1-ramp(s))*Hout + ramp(s)*Hin
            evals, evecs = eigh(H)
            O = evecs.conj().T @ np.column_stack(tracked)   # O[a,b] = <a|tracked_b>
            cost = -np.abs(O)**2
            ri, ci = linear_sum_assignment(cost)
            # ri: eigenstate indices, ci: tracked slot
            order = np.argsort(ci)
            ri = ri[order]
            new_tracked = [evecs[:,ri[b]] for b in range(N)]
            S = np.column_stack(new_tracked).conj().T @ np.column_stack(tracked)
            W = S @ W
            tracked = new_tracked
            assigned = set(ri.tolist())
            othere = [evals[i] for i in range(dim) if i not in assigned]
            mine = [evals[i] for i in assigned]
            gap = min(othere) - max(mine) if max(mine) < min(othere) else 0.0
            # track gap as distance to nearest non-assigned level
            d = min(abs(eo - em) for eo in othere for em in mine)
            mingap = min(mingap, d)

    fin_basis.sort(key=lambda x: x[0])
    finvecs = [v for (q,v) in fin_basis]

        print(\" |C| (no perm):\");   print(np.round(np.abs(C),3))
        print(\" arg(C)/pi:\");       print(np.round(np.angle(C)/np.pi,4))
        print(\" |A| (with perm):\"); print(np.round(np.abs(A),3))
        print(\" arg(A)/pi:\");       print(np.round(np.angle(A)/np.pi,4))

        phis = {(2,3): -2*np.pi*(0+0.3), (1,2): -2*np.pi*(0+0.3),

import fast_mote2 as f
z=np.load('mote2_grid.npz'); E=z['evals']; U=z['evecs']; L=E.shape[0]

            total += 0.5*np.real(np.trace(dP[0]@dP[0]+dP[1]@dP[1]))

# transport each row along n1

The large-\(N\) melonic saddle is the \(q=4\) SYK saddle. Its infrared fermion dimension is

\[
\Delta=\frac14 .
\]

The zero-temperature entropy per Majorana fermion is therefore

\[
\frac{S}{N}
=\frac{\log 2}{2}
-\int_0^{1/4} dx\,\pi\left(\frac12-x\right)\tan(\pi x).
\]

Using \(u=\frac12-x\),

\[
\frac{S}{N}
=\int_0^{1/4}\pi u\cot(\pi u)\,du
=\frac{\log 2}{8}+\frac{G}{2\pi},
\]

where \(G=0.915965594\ldots\) is Catalan’s constant. Thus

\[
\frac{S}{N}=0.232424088\ldots
\]

and to four decimal places,

\[
\boxed{\frac{S}{N}=0.2324}
\]
